extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and prospective buyers/manufacturers/engineers interested in small domestic motors
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating small heat and electric motors
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and comparing the performance, design, safety, cost, and suitability of small heat-engines (gas, oil, Brayton, Otto, Simon, etc.) and electric motors for domestic or light industrial use. Emphasis on fuel economy, steadiness of operation, simplicity, and adaptability to household needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel economy (consumption per indicated horsepower)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amount of fuel used per hour per indicated horsepower (e.g., Otto: 21.5 cubic feet of gas/hour/ihp; Simon: <18 ft; de Bisschof man-power: 11.5 ft/hr; Brayton oil: five gallons in ten hours for a three-horse engine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare machines by their reported fuel consumption and convert to cost given fuel price (example: gas at $2/1000 ft gives ~4 cents/hr/ihp for 21.5 ft). Account for fuel calorific values (petroleum ~double coal) when comparing different fuels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of combustion — gradual combustion vs explosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer combustion that is rapid and gradual rather than an instantaneous explosion, because gradual combustion produces a more continuous, sustained pressure resembling steam-engines and yields better economy and steadiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs that introduce combustible mixture gradually or ignite successive small charges (Simon, Brayton) produce smoother pressure curves and better economy; altering air/gas proportions and using cut-off points can reduce 'explosive' behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression before ignition
rubrics_metrics.description: Compressing the combustible charge prior to ignition increases pressure from expansion (e.g., Otto compresses to one-third original volume before ignition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher compression (within safe limits) promotes efficient expansion and useful pressure; separate compression cylinders (Simon) can help realize better economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilization of waste heat / thermal economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which the heat produced is captured and used rather than lost (e.g., using jacket water to generate steam injected into cylinder to prevent overheating and gain power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engines that recycle jacket/exhaust heat into steam or preheat reservoir water (Simon, attempts cited) show superior economy. Evaluate presence and effectiveness of steam generation from exhaust/jacket heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steadiness and uniformity of speed (governor performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to maintain constant speed under varying loads; quality of the governor and its delicacy (e.g., ordinary ball governor in Otto, Deprez governor sensitive within y⅛ of mean rate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess governor responsiveness, ability to control gas/air admission, and built-in safety features (automatic gas-valve closing if engine stops open).

rubrics_metrics.name: Noise level and silent operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of operational noise (din) produced by the engine; 'silent' designs (Otto silent gas-engine) and mechanical measures (exhaust passed into a chamber) reduce noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer designs with muffled/exhaust-chamber arrangements and those historically described as 'silent' for domestic settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of construction and required workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: How simple the machine is to construct and whether it requires skilled workmanship; simpler designs (gas engines) can be made cheaper and more widely manufactured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate number of precision parts, ease of manufacture, and whether construction demands specialized engineering; simpler machines lower first cost and maintenance skill need.

rubrics_metrics.name: First cost / price and scalability with demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial purchase price relative to power (examples given: Otto $500 for 2hp to $850 for 7hp; Brayton $450 for 3hp, $600 for 5hp; potential to fall to $50 for 1hp with mass production).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both present prices and the prospect of cost reduction with larger demand and competition; weigh first cost against operating cost savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance and operator requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of daily care or skilled operator needed (e.g., some engines require no engineer, automatic oiling systems, some engines can run long periods unattended).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess features like automatic oil delivery, minimal tuning, and start/stop convenience. Reported examples include machines running 47 days unattended and oiling via drip systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lubrication design and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs for oiling moving parts (e.g., oil-cups delivering drops each revolution; piston dipped into oil pan; minimal external oiling needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer reliable, automatic lubrication systems requiring only periodic refill; evaluate accessibility and service intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooling and prevention of overheating
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of water-jackets and circulation to maintain cylinder temperature; cooling that also supplies heat-recovery systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine jacket circulation methods, heat-recovery coupling to steam generation, and whether the cooling approach is compatible with sustained high-efficiency operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaust handling / smokeless/noiseless exhaust
rubrics_metrics.description: How exhaust is expelled and whether it is rendered noiseless or under slight pressure through chambers to reduce noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence of exhaust chambers, back-pressure management, and environmental/comfort impacts for domestic use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size, weight, and floor-space requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical footprint and mass appropriate to intended use (examples: Otto two-horse about 3×7 ft weighing 1400 lb; smaller machines lighter and more compact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the engine can be scaled down to desired domestic footprint and weight; portability (cast one-piece base and ribs avoiding jacket) increases usefulness for household tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for domestic/household use
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the motor's characteristics (simplicity, economy, safety, size, low maintenance) make it appropriate for household tasks like sewing-machines, scroll-saws, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fuel availability, required storage (oil/gas), risk, noise, and whether local regulations/insurance would permit installation in dwellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and fire/explosion hazard (fuel storage and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk associated with the fuel type and storage (e.g., danger from coal-oil storage may increase insurance or be prohibited; gas and oil have different safety profiles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate required on-site fuel quantities, storage safety measures, local building/insurance constraints, and whether small integrated tanks mitigate hazard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to run unattended / reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Durability and capacity for continuous running with little attention (e.g., de Bisschof engine reported running 47 days without stopping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uptime examples, self-oiling systems, and simplicity to judge likelihood of long unattended operation; consider failure modes and safety shutdowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability of fuel (gas vs petroleum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether engine design accepts different fuels and how that affects performance/cost (e.g., Brayton shifted from gas to petroleum vapor for better operation and lower running cost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fuel flexibility, required fuel-handling equipment (vaporizers, jets), and local fuel prices to determine operating economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power delivery characteristics (sustained pressure vs impulsive)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the engine delivers torque/pressure during the stroke — continuous/sustained (steam-like) is preferred to sudden impulsive pressure for economy and smoothness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer engines with cut-off and expansion control that allow the piston to be driven by expanding gases over a good portion of the stroke (Brayton, Simon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of timing and valve/slide-valve actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy of valve timing and slide-valve mechanisms governing intake, ignition, and exhaust (e.g., slide-valve features, channels for ignition and admission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect valve design precision, mechanical linkages (lay-shaft, crank timing), and the potential for leakage or mistiming affecting efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric distribution suitability and motor simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Feasibility and benefits of distributing electricity from a central source for safe, convenient power; electric motors described as largely 'cast-iron and insulated copper wire' and simple to construct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare costs of centralized distribution vs local batteries; weigh simplicity of electric motors and lower skilled manufacturing needs against electricity supply infrastructure and battery economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric motor design for continuous torque (avoidance of dead points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Armature and winding designs that avoid periods of no induced currents (dead points) and produce continuous impulses (e.g., Trouve's spiral-grooved Siemens armature vs standard longitudinal grooves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer armature geometries where parts of the core are approaching/receding during the entire revolution for continuous torque; evaluate commutator and brush arrangements to minimize torque ripple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutator and brush arrangement / speed control in electric motors
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms by which commutator and brushes reverse current and allow regulation (e.g., Deprez design reverses at each half revolution; speed regulated by moving brushes toward neutral points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ease and precision of speed regulation, sensitivity of governor interruptions, and robustness of brushes/commutator under load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-of-power economics (battery vs dynamo/distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative cost and practicality of powering electro-motors from batteries vs distributed current generated centrally (batteries currently very costly per unit power; central distribution favored for continuous power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for operating duration and duty-cycle: batteries feasible for few hours/day, dynamos/distributed supply for sustained industrial/domestic use; consider future technological improvements that might change economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall efficiency relative to steam-engines
rubrics_metrics.description: How closely small motors approach the economy and efficiency of steam-engines of corresponding power (several heat-engines approximate or exceed steam-engine economy depending on fuel and design).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare indicated horsepower fuel costs, calorific values, and effective utilization of heat to benchmark against steam-engine performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portability and design choices that obviate water-jackets
rubrics_metrics.description: Design features (ribs for radiation, one-piece castings) that remove need for water-jackets and make the motor portable and easier to move (advantageous for household use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cooling surface area, radiation capacity, and whether elimination of water-jacket improves portability without sacrificing thermal control.
